summary: Reports test results for a network using the MAP-T double translation approach and gives an overview of how applications behave with a shared IPv4 address. The software came from CERNET and the testbed was on the NIC.br network.

plainLanguage.summary: Experts tried out a way to let many people share one old-style address and wrote down what worked.

questions: how do applications behave with shared ipv4 addresses
how does map-t handle active ftp
why do some applications fail with map-t
how well does map-t perform compared to nat
subtitle: What happens when many users share one IPv4 address through double translation

tldr.problem: As IPv4 addresses run out, networks must let many users share single addresses. MAP-T is a double translation technique that translates IPv4 to IPv6 at the edge, crossing an IPv6-only network, then translates back to IPv4 at the other end. This RFC tests whether common applications actually work in such a network.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC.br network in Brazil built a testbed with MAP-T core, IPv6-only router, and CPE devices running CERNET MAP-T software. Machines running Linux, Windows 7, and Windows XP sent traffic through the double translation while accessing common websites, video streaming, chat applications, file transfers, and other services.
tldr.outcome: Most applications worked well, including browsers, email, video streaming, and instant messaging. A few failed: command-line FTP in active mode, traceroute, and BitTorrent seeding. User experience was reported as very good with no special configuration needed.

today: RFC 7703 is an Informational RFC documenting practical testing of MAP-T in 2015. MAP-T and its variant MAP-E (RFC 7597, RFC 7599) remain standards for IPv4 address sharing in IPv6-only networks. The techniques are deployed in some IPv6 transition networks, though the adoption rate varies by region and operator. The testing remains relevant as networks continue IPv6 deployment and IPv4 addresses continue to be exhausted.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
MAP-T (Mapping of Address and Port using Translation) is a technique for letting many IPv6-only devices share a limited pool of IPv4 addresses. It works by translating IPv4 packets to IPv6 at the customer edge, routing them across an IPv6-only core network, then translating them back to IPv4 at the other end. This document reports on practical testing of MAP-T using common applications on three operating systems: Linux (Ubuntu 12.04), Windows 7, and Windows XP.

The test network was built on the NIC.br network in Brazil, using MAP-T software (version 1.1) from CERNET. The topology included a MAP-T core, an IPv6-only router, MAP-T CPE devices at the customer premises, and host machines running the test operating systems. Hosts received only IPv4 addresses with IPv6 disabled to ensure the translation was being tested, not bypassed.
sections.plainLanguage: A group set up a test network where computers could only use one old-style address that was shared with many others. The network automatically translated these addresses back and forth so computers on both sides could talk. They tried all the things people normally do on the internet to see if it worked.

sections.title: Network Topology and Configuration
sections.content:
The testbed network had four main components. The MAP-T Core handled translation from IPv4 to IPv6, using the IPv6 prefix 2001:db8:6:d600::/56 and IPv4 prefix 198.51.100.248/29. An IPv6-only Router connected the MAP-T core to the customer premises equipment, carrying all traffic over IPv6 between them. The MAP-T CPE at each customer location translated IPv6 back to IPv4 for the host. Host machines configured with IPv4 address 198.51.100.250/29, gateway 198.51.100.249, and DNS 8.8.8.8 received traffic through this double translation.

All machines were virtualized except the physical IPv6 router, running on the NIC.br's real IPv4 and IPv6 networks. The configuration files specified prefix sizes, interface addresses, and routing rules. The MAP-T software used an index variable (-R 16) and offset variable (-M 2) to map ports across shared addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Four pieces: one that changes old-style addresses to new-style, one that moves data on the new-style network, one that changes it back, and the host computer that does normal internet stuff.

sections.title: Application Testing Results
sections.content:
The testing evaluated 45 different applications and websites in ten categories. Browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Internet Explorer, Safari, Lynx) all passed without modification. Web browsing of Google.com and MSN.com worked. Web dynamic content including Flash, Silverlight, Java applets, and HTML5 websites all passed. Video streaming from YouTube, Dailymotion, and Zappiens.br all worked. Social networking (Facebook, Twitter) passed. Webmail (Gmail, Hotmail) passed. Chat (UOL chat rooms) passed. Image hosting (Flickr) passed.

In the communication protocol category, Skype, Google Talk, Jabber (XMPP), MSN Messenger, and IRC all worked. Torrent clients (Vuze, uTorrent, Ktorrent) partially passed: they could download but not seed or share files because incoming connections are not possible through MAP-T. Remote access tools showed mixed results: SSH passed, command-line FTP failed in active mode (but FileZilla FTP and wget passed), and standard FTP had issues in passive mode on Windows. Antivirus updates (Avira, AVG, Avast) all passed. Media players and streaming (VLC, RealPlayer, Windows Media Player) all passed. Network tools showed issues: ping outbound passed, but ping inbound, traceroute, and tracert all failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Testers tried 45 different programs and websites. Almost all of them worked perfectly. Only a few that need special network tricks (like telling the server to connect back to you, or tracing the path to the server) had problems.

sections.title: Analysis and Limitations
sections.content:
User experience was reported as very good. Network delay, streaming experience, and download time were similar to a network using IPv4 addresses with traditional NAT44 on the CPE. No special configuration was needed for working applications.

The failures were well understood. Traceroute and tracert do not work because there is no continuity of the IPv4 network: the path crosses an IPv6-only network that the tools cannot detect. Command-line FTP in active mode fails because active mode requires incoming connections to specific ports without an outbound connection on those ports first. Passive mode FTP (including FileZilla) works because it uses outbound connections only. BitTorrent applications cannot seed or share files because MAP-T version 1.1 uses NAT44 on the CPE, which blocks incoming connections even on ports assigned to the host by the address-plus-port division.

The CERNET team provided feedback and developed MAP-T version 2.2c, which supports incoming connections on specific ports in each CPE, addressing the seeding limitation.
sections.plainLanguage: The few failures were not due to the translation itself but to applications that need special networking tricks. The translation system worked as well as the old way of sharing addresses.

sections.title: Future Testing and Conclusions
sections.content:
Future testing should consider Mapping of Address and Port with Encapsulation (MAP-E), which is now supported in newer versions of CERNET MAP software and may handle some edge cases better. Additional operating systems (Mac OS, Android, iOS) and devices (mobile phones, tablets, gaming consoles) could be tested. The impact of different port-sharing ratios on performance and functionality should be measured. Results from the MAP Interoperability Testing document (RFC 7597 and others) are relevant. Impact on DNS and DNSSEC could be verified as well.

The testing demonstrates that MAP-T is viable for typical user applications, with performance and user experience comparable to traditional shared address translation schemes. The failures encountered are not fundamental limitations of double translation but rather expected behavior when applications depend on abilities that any NAT blocks (active FTP, inbound connections for seeding, traceroute visibility into IPv6 networks).
sections.plainLanguage: The test showed that the translation method works fine for everyday internet use. Future tests could try it on phones, tablets, and more recent software to see if that changes the results.
